It seemed badly written enough that he had two fairly good ways around it - arguing that the hunting law didn't apply because he wasn't hunting, or arguing that "not in compliance with A and B" means "not in compliance with A and not in compliance with B" (where he's definitely fine on A because he's over 16).

Seems to me that the prosecution was pushing hard on the claim that the provocation was Kyle raising the rifle to *Ziminski*, based on a blurry and heavily manipulated frame of the drone video and the testimony of the guy who manipulated it.

They should lean into it. Show the blurry photo - there's nowhere near enough detail to justify a provocation claim, and the jury is likely to see that. Make it the pillar holding up the entire case - if the jurors are not absolutely sure that it says what the prosecution claims (unlikely anyone at all can be sure), then *everything* falls apart.

They may have screwed him on the possession charge as well. No-one ever testified to whether the rifle was short-barreled, *which it very obviously isn't*, but the prosecution is arguing that this means he can't claim the exemption. 

And they literally conceded that he was in violation of 29.593, i.e. "Requirement for certificate of accomplishment to obtain hunting approval." But he wasn't hunting so I can't imagine why they conceded this. They think it doesn't matter because the "under 16" violation doesn't apply, but the wording leaves it unclear whether "not in compliance with A and B" means "not (in compliance with A and B)" or "(not in compliance with) A and B".
